questions.q: According to this lesson, what do most real-world breaches actually exploit?
options: Known, already-patched vulnerabilities on systems that never got the update
Hardware defects that no software patch could ever fix
Only vulnerabilities in operating systems released within the last week
Vulnerabilities that have never been discovered by anyone before
questions.explain: A huge share of breaches exploit flaws the vendor already fixed months or years earlier, on machines that simply never installed the patch.

options: An unofficial term with no connection to any real Microsoft release schedule
Microsoft's practice of releasing most security updates on the second Tuesday of every month
The day Linux distributions coordinate a joint patch release
A once-a-year event where all Windows updates for the year are released at once
questions.explain: Microsoft adopted this monthly, predictable cadence so IT departments could plan testing and deployment around a known schedule.

options: A patch that only applies to out-of-support operating systems
A patch that disables Patch Tuesday permanently once installed
A patch delivered only through physical media, never downloaded
A patch released outside the normal monthly cycle because a vulnerability is too severe to wait
questions.explain: Microsoft breaks from the regular cadence for vulnerabilities severe enough — such as active exploitation in the wild — that waiting for the next scheduled Tuesday would leave too wide a gap.

questions.q: What does the informal term "Exploit Wednesday" refer to?
options: A Linux-only phenomenon with no Windows equivalent
The day Microsoft officially retires old patches
Attackers reverse-engineering a newly released patch within days to build an exploit against unpatched systems
A second, unofficial Patch Tuesday that occurs every Wednesday
questions.explain: Once a patch ships, comparing the patched and unpatched files (patch diffing) can reveal exactly what vulnerability was fixed, often within days.

questions.q: Why do organizations typically deploy a new patch to a pilot ring before rolling it out broadly?
options: Because vendors legally require a pilot ring before any deployment
Because pilot rings are the only machines capable of receiving updates
To balance the need to close the exposure window quickly against the risk of an untested patch breaking production systems
To slow down deployment indefinitely with no real security benefit
questions.explain: A staged rollout lets IT watch a small test group for problems before pushing the same update to the entire fleet, managing the speed-vs-stability tension deliberately.
